Azriel
AZ-ree-el
n. (three men: a chief in Manasseh, a ruler of Naphtali under David, and the father of Jeremiah's pursuer)
Hebrew Azriel, help of God, or God is my help, from azar, to help, and El, God; borne by three men, 1 Chronicles 5:24, 27:19, Jeremiah 36:26.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Azriel means God is my help, and it is given to three men whose circumstances differ sharply. The first is a tribal chief east of Jordan: “And these were the heads of the house of their fathers, even Epher, and Ishi, and Eliel, and Azriel, and Jeremiah, and Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of the house of their fathers” (1 Chronicles 5:24). The second is remembered through his son in David's administration: “of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel” (1 Chronicles 27:19). The third stands on the wrong side of a famous scene. When Jehoiakim had burned the scroll, “the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet: but the LORD hid them” (Jeremiah 36:26). The princes had already warned the two men — “Then said the princes unto Baruch, Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah; and let no man know where ye be” (Jeremiah 36:19) — and the name of the man sent to arrest the prophet is the son of one called help of God. The irony is the text's own, and the help went to the hunted.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Azriel, help of God, or God is my help; borne by a Manassite chief, by the father of David's ruler over Naphtali, and by the father of one sent to seize Jeremiah.

Hebrew Azriel, help of God, or God is my help.

From azar, to help or succour, with El, God.

It occurs three times in the Authorized Version: 1 Chronicles 5:24, 1 Chronicles 27:19, and Jeremiah 36:26.

The first was a head of a father's house among the tribes east of Jordan.

The third was father of Seraiah, whom Jehoiakim sent to take Baruch and Jeremiah.

Key Scripture

1Ch 5:24 — "And these were the heads of the house of their fathers, even Epher, and Ishi, and Eliel, and Azriel, and Jeremiah, and Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of the house of their fathers."

1Ch 27:19 — "Of Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah: of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel:"

Jer 36:26 — "But the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet: but the LORD hid them."

Jer 36:19 — "Then said the princes unto Baruch, Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah; and let no man know where ye be."

Modern Corruption

Divine help is reduced to a feeling of support; the name is attached in Scripture to men on both sides of a persecution, and the help proves to be God's own hiding of His prophet.

expand to see more

Therapeutic religion treats help from God as inward reassurance, so a name meaning God is my help is heard as a sentiment about how the bearer felt. Jeremiah 36 refuses that reading. The help in question is concrete and external: a king issues an arrest warrant, officers go out, and “the LORD hid them”. Divine help there is an act in history with a result you could verify by looking for two men and failing to find them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a godly name is no guarantee of a godly house, and no obstacle to God's purpose. Seraiah son of Azriel carried a warrant against the word of God; the scroll he was sent to suppress was rewritten with more added to it. The preservation of Scripture does not depend on the goodwill of the men who handle it, and the help named in Azriel belonged, that day, to the prophet and not to the officer.
